screens.title: Asynchronous Communication: Message Queues
screens.narratorSegment: In distributed systems, not every interaction needs an immediate reply. Message queues let services hand off work without waiting, so producers keep running and consumers process work independently. In this lesson you will learn the core parts of a message queue system—producers, consumers, queues and the broker—and why that separation matters. We’ll examine two main patterns: point-to-point, where each message is consumed once, and publish/subscribe, where an event fans out to many subscribers. You will also see how queues provide load leveling so spikes don’t overwhelm workers, and what operational controls—message durability, acknowledgments, and dead-letter queues—are needed to avoid lost data. As an example, imagine an online store: when an order is placed the Order Service publishes an event and payment, inventory, and notification services independently react. By the end of this board you’ll be able to describe that flow, pick the right pattern for common use cases, and name the safety features required to run a reliable broker.

Use message queues to decouple services, buffer work, and improve resilience.

Visual concept

Consumer
Retrieves, processes and acknowledges messages when durable processing is required.
Why this matters
Message queues are a practical mechanism to make systems resilient to outages and variable load without merging service responsibilities. They are widely used for background jobs, event distribution and buffering spikes in production systems.

screens.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication
screens.narratorSegment: Synchronous request-response patterns like REST or gRPC block the caller until a reply arrives. That tight coupling makes the caller sensitive to the callee’s latency and failures. By contrast, asynchronous patterns using message queues let the producer hand off work and continue without waiting. This changes system behavior in three important ways. First, availability: a producer can succeed even if the consumer is temporarily unavailable because the broker stores the message. Second, resilience: failures are isolated and don’t cascade across services. Third, elasticity: consumers can scale independently and process a backlog at their own pace. A common example is a web request that triggers image processing. If the request waits for the processing job, the user faces long latency. With a queue, the web service publishes a task and immediately responds, while a pool of workers consumes tasks and completes the job asynchronously. A common misconception is that queues always add complexity; they do add operational overhead, but the trade-off is reduced coupling and improved fault tolerance for long-running or non-critical operations. Consider when immediate user feedback is required; in those cases synchronous calls are still the right choice. How will you decide between latency and resilience in your designs?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Synchronous vs Asynchronous
Comparison

Blocking (Sync)

Caller waits for a response; tight coupling and synchronous failure propagation.
When to use
Short, immediate operations where latency matters and immediate feedback is required.
Common pitfall
Blocking causes cascading failures if downstream services are slow or unavailable.
Comparison

Asynchronous (Queues)

Producer enqueues work and continues; consumers process at their pace and acknowledge successful work.
When to use
Long-running jobs, background processing, event propagation, and buffering spikes.
Common pitfall
Assuming ordering and delivery without configuring durability, acks and DLQs can lead to surprises.
Concrete example
Web server publishes an image-processing task to a queue and immediately returns a confirmation to the user; workers consume tasks and update status when complete.
Misconception
Queues automatically make systems reliable; they help only when durability and acknowledgments are correctly configured.
Key Takeaway

Pick synchronous for immediate responses. Use queues to decouple, buffer, and recover from partial failures.

screens.title: Key Components of a Message Queue System
screens.narratorSegment: A message queue system has a small set of well-defined roles. The producer or publisher creates messages and sends them to the broker; producers do not need to know which consumers will handle the messages. A consumer or subscriber connects to the broker and pulls or receives messages to process. The queue is the broker-managed buffer that holds messages until a consumer acknowledges them. The broker is the server component that stores, routes and delivers messages; it offers features like persistence, routing rules, topics or exchanges, and management APIs. In practice, brokers like RabbitMQ, Apache ActiveMQ, Amazon SQS and Azure Service Bus provide configurable durability, acknowledgement semantics, and dead-letter queues. A concrete example is an order event: the Order Service publishes a JSON message to an order topic; Payment, Inventory and Notification services each subscribe and independently process the message. A common misconception is that producers and consumers must be written in the same language or run on the same platform—message queues explicitly avoid that requirement. Remember: design your message contents to be version-tolerant and idempotent to make consumers resilient to retries and reprocessing.

keyIdea.title: Component roles
keyIdea.text: Producers send messages; brokers store and route them; queues buffer; consumers retrieve and acknowledge processing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Components
Definition

Who does what

Clear responsibilities help design robust flows and allow independent scaling and deployment.
Producer (Publisher)
Creates messages and hands them to the broker without waiting for processing.
Broker / Queue
Stores and routes messages; may provide topics, exchanges and durability options.
Consumer (Subscriber)
Consumes messages and acknowledges successful processing to the broker.
Example flow
Order placed → Message published
Order Service publishes an OrderPlaced message to the broker. The broker stores it in a topic or queue and routes copies to subscribers as configured.
Subscribers process independently
Payment service charges the card, Inventory deducts stock, Notification sends confirmation. Each service handles retries and acknowledgments separately.
Design tip
Keep message schemas backward compatible and make consumers idempotent to tolerate retries.
Pitfall
Assuming broker defaults guarantee durability — confirm persistence settings for production workloads.

screens.title: Message Lifecycle and Decoupling
screens.narratorSegment: A message follows a clear lifecycle: creation, enqueue, delivery, processing, acknowledgment or retry, and possibly dead-lettering. When the producer creates a message, it publishes to the broker which persists it to a queue or topic. When a consumer becomes available, it retrieves the message and attempts processing. If processing succeeds, the consumer acknowledges the message so the broker can remove it. If it fails, the broker may redeliver, postpone, or move the message to a dead-letter queue after configurable retries. This lifecycle supports decoupling because the producer and consumer never need to be online simultaneously; the broker intermediates and stores state. A concrete scenario is a payment that retries on transient network issues: the consumer should detect transient errors and let the broker requeue the message for retry, while permanent errors are moved to a dead-letter queue for inspection. A common misconception is that brokers automatically handle retries the way you need—retry policies, backoff strategies, and DLQ thresholds must be designed per workflow. Your takeaway: explicitly define acknowledgment and retry semantics when designing message flows so you get the durability and behavior your system requires.

keyIdea.title: Lifecycle insight
keyIdea.text: Design explicit publish, ack, retry and DLQ behaviors so messages are reliably processed and errors are surfaced for inspection.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Message Lifecycle
Process Flow

Publish → Store → Deliver → Ack

A clear lifecycle prevents silent failures and defines the retry behavior you expect.
1. Publish
Producer sends a message to the broker; broker may persist it to disk if durability is enabled.
2. Enqueue
Broker queues or routes the message to topics/exchanges according to configuration.
3. Deliver & Process
Consumer retrieves and processes; processing must be idempotent to handle retries.
4. Acknowledge or Retry
Consumer acks on success; on failure the broker retries or sends to a dead-letter queue after limits are reached.
Concrete example
Payment processing: if a transient gateway error occurs, worker fails and broker requeues message. After configured retries the message moves to a dead-letter queue for manual inspection.
Common mistake
Relying on default retry policies without thinking about idempotency and backoff can multiply load on failing services.
Key Takeaway

Define ack, retry and DLQ behavior early to meet your reliability goals and avoid hidden message loss.

screens.title: Point-to-Point vs Publish/Subscribe
screens.narratorSegment: Message systems support two primary patterns. Point-to-point delivers each message to a single consumer and removes it after processing. It’s ideal for distributing work across a pool of workers where exactly one worker should perform each task, like image resizing jobs or payment attempts. Publish/subscribe, on the other hand, broadcasts each message to every subscriber. It is ideal for events that multiple services must react to, such as order placed notifications that trigger payment, inventory and notification services. When evaluating which to use, consider whether tasks must be processed once or whether multiple independent actions must occur. A common misconception is that pub/sub guarantees ordering across all subscribers; individual brokers may provide ordering per partition or queue, but global ordering across multiple subscribers or partitions often requires additional design. Another operational difference is scaling: point-to-point scales worker pools to increase throughput, while pub/sub scales subscribers independently. When architects design an e-commerce order flow, they often publish an event to a topic so multiple services receive the same message and act independently. Which pattern will your use case demand—single responsibility or broadcast?

keyIdea.title: Pattern choice
keyIdea.text: Point-to-point for single-worker tasks; pub/sub for broadcasting events to multiple services that act independently.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Patterns
Point-to-Point

One message, one consumer

Use for task queues where each task should be processed exactly once by one worker.
Example
A pool of workers consumes jobs and each job is performed by a single worker.
Scaling
Increase worker count to improve throughput; messages are balanced across workers.
Publish/Subscribe

One message, many subscribers

Use for events that multiple services need to consume independently.
Example
An OrderPlaced event is delivered to Payment, Inventory and Notification services simultaneously.
Scaling
Subscribers scale independently; each receives its own copy of the message.
Design tip
Pick pub/sub for fan-out; pick point-to-point for distributing work among workers.
Misconception
Pub/sub doesn’t guarantee global ordering across multiple subscribers without careful partitioning.
Key Takeaway

Match the messaging pattern to the interaction intent: single-worker tasks or many independent listeners.

screens.title: Common Use Cases for Message Queues
screens.narratorSegment: Message queues are applied in several recurring ways. Asynchronous task processing offloads long-running work — image conversion, video encoding or report generation — from the main request flow so user-facing services remain responsive. Decoupling microservices allows teams to change and deploy services independently; producers simply publish events and consumers evolve separately. Event-driven architectures use topics to propagate state changes like user registered or order placed to any interested service. Load leveling collects bursts of incoming requests into a queue so downstream services can process at a steady rate and avoid crashes during spikes. Batch processing benefits from queues by collecting records over time and processing them periodically. Consider the order example: Order Service publishes an event and payment, inventory and notification services each process it. A potential misconception is treating every background task as safe to run exactly once; you must enforce idempotency and design for at-least-once delivery unless your broker and processing guarantees provide strictly-once semantics. These use cases guide your choice of broker features and operational practices. Common Use Cases for Message Queues means use queues for background work, service decoupling, event distribution and smoothing traffic spikes while ensuring idempotency and safe retries.. In practical terms, background jobs, decoupling microservices, events, and batch processing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Use Cases

Where queues help most

Common production uses that benefit from decoupling and buffering.
Asynchronous Task Processing
Offload slow work like encoding or batch reports so the frontend stays responsive.
Decoupling Microservices
Publish events and let independent services subscribe and react without tight integration.
Event-Driven Architectures
Propagate domain events to multiple services for eventual consistency and analytics.
Load Leveling & Batch Processing
Buffer bursts and aggregate messages for periodic processing to match downstream capacity.
Concrete scenario
Order placed event: Order Service publishes to a topic. Payment verifies charge, Inventory adjusts stock, Notification sends emails. Each service processes independently and can retry or fail without blocking the others.
Design caution
Make operations idempotent because retries and redeliveries are normal in many broker setups.

screens.title: Durability, Acknowledgments, and Dead-Letter Queues
screens.narratorSegment: Reliability in a message system depends on three important mechanisms. Message durability ensures that the broker persists messages to disk so a broker crash does not drop in-flight messages. Consumer acknowledgments tell the broker that a message was processed successfully and can be removed; without explicit acks the broker may assume failure and redeliver. Dead-letter queues capture messages that cannot be processed after configured retries, allowing manual inspection or special handling. In practice you must decide which messages need persistent storage, what acknowledgment model to use, and how many retries to attempt before dead-lettering. For example, a payment message should be durable and require acknowledgment only when payment is confirmed, while a telemetry event might be allowed to be best-effort. A common mistake is assuming once an ack is sent the work is durable on the consumer side; ack only indicates the broker can forget the message, not that downstream side effects are persisted. Therefore, design the consumer to persist results before acknowledging when necessary, or use transactional features where the broker and consumer support them. These choices determine your system’s tolerance for broker or consumer failures.

keyIdea.title: Reliability controls
keyIdea.text: Enable durability, require explicit acknowledgments, and route unprocessable messages to a dead-letter queue to avoid silent loss.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Durability & Safety

Durability, Acks, DLQs

These three features form the backbone of message safety and observability.
Message Durability
Persist messages to disk so a broker restart doesn’t lose queued work.
Consumer Acknowledgment
Consumers ack on successful processing so brokers can safely remove messages.
Dead-Letter Queues
Messages that repeatedly fail are routed to DLQs for later inspection and remediation.
Concrete guidance
Decide durability per message type, persist consumer side effects before acking when necessary, and use DLQs to isolate poison messages for manual handling.
Common mistake
Treating ack as a guarantee that downstream actions are durable. Ack means the broker can drop the message; ensure consumer persistence first.

screens.title: Ordering, Delivery Semantics, and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Message ordering and delivery semantics are essential design considerations. FIFO preserves insertion order, but in distributed brokers strict global ordering is difficult and may require single partitions or careful routing. Delivery semantics typically fall into at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once categories. Most brokers default to at-least-once delivery where messages can be redelivered if a consumer crashes before acknowledging. This requires idempotent consumers so repeated processing does not corrupt state. Exactly-once processing is hard and often requires transactional integration between broker and consumer or external coordination. Common mistakes include ignoring the need for idempotency, assuming acknowledgments imply durable side effects, and not configuring persistence for critical message types. Another frequent oversight is not instrumenting broker health and queue lengths; queues growing unexpectedly is an early sign of downstream trouble. To design correctly, choose the delivery semantics you need, make consumers idempotent for at-least-once, and adopt monitoring and DLQs to detect and handle problematic messages. Ask yourself: what happens if a message is processed twice or out of order in my system? In practical terms, understand fifo, at-least-once, and typical pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Ordering & Delivery

Define ordering needs and choose delivery semantics that match your correctness requirements.
FIFO (Ordering)
Preserves order but often requires single partition or queue, which can limit throughput.
At-least-once
Messages may be delivered more than once; consumers must be idempotent.
Exactly-once (hard)
Requires transactional guarantees or de-duplication strategies across broker and consumer.
Common mistakes
  • Not making consumers idempotent for at-least-once delivery.
  • Assuming acks guarantee durable downstream effects.
  • Ignoring monitoring and queue length alerts until a backlog becomes critical.
Key Takeaway

Plan for duplicate deliveries and monitor queue health; choose ordering guarantees only when necessary due to throughput trade-offs.

screens.title: Operational Considerations: Scaling and Security
screens.narratorSegment: Running message brokers in production requires operational planning. Scale brokers by partitioning topics or sharding queues, and scale consumers independently to match throughput. Monitor queue lengths, consumer lag and error rates—growing queues are an early indicator of downstream trouble. Configure retry backoff and dead-letter routing to avoid amplifying load on failing consumers. On the security side, enable authentication and authorization so only trusted services can publish or subscribe to topics and queues. Encrypt sensitive payloads or use transport-level encryption offered by the broker. Backups, persistence configuration, and broker clustering or managed broker services help with high availability. A common operational mistake is treating brokers like a black box: you must tune persistence, memory limits, and retention to fit your workload. Also instrument end-to-end: trace messages through the system and capture metadata such as message age and retry counts. The practical result is predictable throughput, early failure detection, and policy-driven protection for sensitive messages. Scaling & Monitoring

Partition topics, shard queues, and scale consumers; watch metrics to detect backlogs early.
Scale
Partition or shard to increase parallelism; scale consumer pools to consume backlog.
Monitor
Track queue length, consumer lag, retry counts and DLQ activity as primary signals.
Backpressure
Use throttling and adaptive scaling to avoid overwhelming consumers when spikes occur.

Security & Availability

Require authentication and authorization for producers and consumers, encrypt transport or payloads for sensitive data, and use clustering or managed brokers for high availability.
Operational pitfall
Not tuning persistence and retention can cause memory pressure or unexpected message loss during restarts.

Design Checklist

Run these checks before adopting a queue for a use case.
  1. Confirm async interaction intent: is immediate reply required?
  2. Choose pattern: point-to-point or publish/subscribe.
  3. Set durability and acknowledgment semantics per message type.
  4. Design consumers to be idempotent for retries.
  5. Configure DLQs and retry/backoff strategies.
  6. Instrument queue length, lag and retry counts; set alerts.
  7. Secure broker access and encrypt sensitive payloads.
  8. Plan partitions, shards and consumer autoscaling for throughput.
Common mistake
Skipping idempotency and monitoring leads to hidden failures and unbounded backlogs.
Key Takeaway

A short checklist reduces deployment surprises: validate intent, safety, and observability before launch.

fullNarratorScript:
In distributed systems, not every interaction needs an immediate reply. Message queues let services hand off work without waiting, so producers keep running and consumers process work independently. In this lesson you will learn the core parts of a message queue system—producers, consumers, queues and the broker—and why that separation matters. We’ll examine two main patterns: point-to-point, where each message is consumed once, and publish/subscribe, where an event fans out to many subscribers. You will also see how queues provide load leveling so spikes don’t overwhelm workers, and what operational controls—message durability, acknowledgments, and dead-letter queues—are needed to avoid lost data. As an example, imagine an online store: when an order is placed the Order Service publishes an event and payment, inventory, and notification services independently react. By the end of this board you’ll be able to describe that flow, pick the right pattern for common use cases, and name the safety features required to run a reliable broker.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to describe how message-oriented middleware works and why teams use queues. First, you’ll understand core principles and benefits: how decoupling and buffering improve resilience and how queues fit into event-driven architectures. You will also be able to identify the four key components of a queue system—producer, consumer, queue, and broker—and explain their responsibilities. Next, you will clearly explain how queues provide fault tolerance and load leveling, and when those properties matter for long-running tasks or traffic spikes. Finally, you will differentiate the two primary messaging patterns — point-to-point and publish/subscribe — and select which pattern fits common scenarios such as task distribution or broadcasting events. Each objective is tied to practical examples like order processing so you can map theory to real system design decisions.

These objectives focus you on applied outcomes. You will learn to identify when asynchronous queues are the right choice, such as when work is long-running or when a service should not block on another. You will also practice mapping producers and consumers in real flows and choosing queues or topics according to how many services need each message. You will test your designs against failure scenarios: how to keep messages safe with durability, how acknowledgments ensure at-least-once or exactly-once semantics in practice, and when to use dead-letter queues for problematic messages. Finally, you’ll recognize typical use cases—background tasks, event-driven updates, and batch processing—so you can recommend a sensible queue pattern to a team. Each card represents a verifiable skill you can demonstrate with an architectural sketch or a short sequence of messages.

Synchronous request-response patterns like REST or gRPC block the caller until a reply arrives. That tight coupling makes the caller sensitive to the callee’s latency and failures. By contrast, asynchronous patterns using message queues let the producer hand off work and continue without waiting. This changes system behavior in three important ways. First, availability: a producer can succeed even if the consumer is temporarily unavailable because the broker stores the message. Second, resilience: failures are isolated and don’t cascade across services. Third, elasticity: consumers can scale independently and process a backlog at their own pace. A common example is a web request that triggers image processing. If the request waits for the processing job, the user faces long latency. With a queue, the web service publishes a task and immediately responds, while a pool of workers consumes tasks and completes the job asynchronously. A common misconception is that queues always add complexity; they do add operational overhead, but the trade-off is reduced coupling and improved fault tolerance for long-running or non-critical operations. Consider when immediate user feedback is required; in those cases synchronous calls are still the right choice. How will you decide between latency and resilience in your designs?

A message queue system has a small set of well-defined roles. The producer or publisher creates messages and sends them to the broker; producers do not need to know which consumers will handle the messages. A consumer or subscriber connects to the broker and pulls or receives messages to process. The queue is the broker-managed buffer that holds messages until a consumer acknowledges them. The broker is the server component that stores, routes and delivers messages; it offers features like persistence, routing rules, topics or exchanges, and management APIs. In practice, brokers like RabbitMQ, Apache ActiveMQ, Amazon SQS and Azure Service Bus provide configurable durability, acknowledgement semantics, and dead-letter queues. A concrete example is an order event: the Order Service publishes a JSON message to an order topic; Payment, Inventory and Notification services each subscribe and independently process the message. A common misconception is that producers and consumers must be written in the same language or run on the same platform—message queues explicitly avoid that requirement. Remember: design your message contents to be version-tolerant and idempotent to make consumers resilient to retries and reprocessing.

A message follows a clear lifecycle: creation, enqueue, delivery, processing, acknowledgment or retry, and possibly dead-lettering. When the producer creates a message, it publishes to the broker which persists it to a queue or topic. When a consumer becomes available, it retrieves the message and attempts processing. If processing succeeds, the consumer acknowledges the message so the broker can remove it. If it fails, the broker may redeliver, postpone, or move the message to a dead-letter queue after configurable retries. This lifecycle supports decoupling because the producer and consumer never need to be online simultaneously; the broker intermediates and stores state. A concrete scenario is a payment that retries on transient network issues: the consumer should detect transient errors and let the broker requeue the message for retry, while permanent errors are moved to a dead-letter queue for inspection. A common misconception is that brokers automatically handle retries the way you need—retry policies, backoff strategies, and DLQ thresholds must be designed per workflow. Your takeaway: explicitly define acknowledgment and retry semantics when designing message flows so you get the durability and behavior your system requires.

Message systems support two primary patterns. Point-to-point delivers each message to a single consumer and removes it after processing. It’s ideal for distributing work across a pool of workers where exactly one worker should perform each task, like image resizing jobs or payment attempts. Publish/subscribe, on the other hand, broadcasts each message to every subscriber. It is ideal for events that multiple services must react to, such as order placed notifications that trigger payment, inventory and notification services. When evaluating which to use, consider whether tasks must be processed once or whether multiple independent actions must occur. A common misconception is that pub/sub guarantees ordering across all subscribers; individual brokers may provide ordering per partition or queue, but global ordering across multiple subscribers or partitions often requires additional design. Another operational difference is scaling: point-to-point scales worker pools to increase throughput, while pub/sub scales subscribers independently. When architects design an e-commerce order flow, they often publish an event to a topic so multiple services receive the same message and act independently. Which pattern will your use case demand—single responsibility or broadcast?

Message queues are applied in several recurring ways. Asynchronous task processing offloads long-running work — image conversion, video encoding or report generation — from the main request flow so user-facing services remain responsive. Decoupling microservices allows teams to change and deploy services independently; producers simply publish events and consumers evolve separately. Event-driven architectures use topics to propagate state changes like user registered or order placed to any interested service. Load leveling collects bursts of incoming requests into a queue so downstream services can process at a steady rate and avoid crashes during spikes. Batch processing benefits from queues by collecting records over time and processing them periodically. Consider the order example: Order Service publishes an event and payment, inventory and notification services each process it. A potential misconception is treating every background task as safe to run exactly once; you must enforce idempotency and design for at-least-once delivery unless your broker and processing guarantees provide strictly-once semantics. These use cases guide your choice of broker features and operational practices. Common Use Cases for Message Queues means use queues for background work, service decoupling, event distribution and smoothing traffic spikes while ensuring idempotency and safe retries.. In practical terms, background jobs, decoupling microservices, events, and batch processing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reliability in a message system depends on three important mechanisms. Message durability ensures that the broker persists messages to disk so a broker crash does not drop in-flight messages. Consumer acknowledgments tell the broker that a message was processed successfully and can be removed; without explicit acks the broker may assume failure and redeliver. Dead-letter queues capture messages that cannot be processed after configured retries, allowing manual inspection or special handling. In practice you must decide which messages need persistent storage, what acknowledgment model to use, and how many retries to attempt before dead-lettering. For example, a payment message should be durable and require acknowledgment only when payment is confirmed, while a telemetry event might be allowed to be best-effort. A common mistake is assuming once an ack is sent the work is durable on the consumer side; ack only indicates the broker can forget the message, not that downstream side effects are persisted. Therefore, design the consumer to persist results before acknowledging when necessary, or use transactional features where the broker and consumer support them. These choices determine your system’s tolerance for broker or consumer failures.

Message ordering and delivery semantics are essential design considerations. FIFO preserves insertion order, but in distributed brokers strict global ordering is difficult and may require single partitions or careful routing. Delivery semantics typically fall into at-least-once, at-most-once, and exactly-once categories. Most brokers default to at-least-once delivery where messages can be redelivered if a consumer crashes before acknowledging. This requires idempotent consumers so repeated processing does not corrupt state. Exactly-once processing is hard and often requires transactional integration between broker and consumer or external coordination. Common mistakes include ignoring the need for idempotency, assuming acknowledgments imply durable side effects, and not configuring persistence for critical message types. Another frequent oversight is not instrumenting broker health and queue lengths; queues growing unexpectedly is an early sign of downstream trouble. To design correctly, choose the delivery semantics you need, make consumers idempotent for at-least-once, and adopt monitoring and DLQs to detect and handle problematic messages.
